summary: Vermont's independent senator since 2007, after eight years as Burlington's socialist mayor and 16 in the House, and the longest-serving independent in congressional history. His 2016 and 2020 presidential campaigns made him the leader of the Democratic left; since 2025 his "Fighting Oligarchy" tour with Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has drawn crowds of up to 36,000, and his resolutions to block arms sales to Israel won the votes of 40 members of the Democratic caucus in April 2026.

chapters.title: Brooklyn, Chicago and Vermont
chapters.dek: A Holocaust survivor's son turned civil-rights activist and third-party candidate.
chapters.body:
Sanders was born in Brooklyn on September 8, 1941, to a Polish-Jewish immigrant father whose family, he has said, "was wiped out by Hitler in the Holocaust" [[wikipedia, toi-jewish-2016]]. After a year at Brooklyn College he transferred to the University of Chicago, where he joined civil-rights protests with CORE and SNCC, including a 1962 sit-in, and attended the 1963 March on Washington; he graduated in 1964 [[wikipedia, sanders-senate-bio]].

He moved to Vermont in 1968 and ran for governor and the Senate as a Liberty Union candidate between 1972 and 1976 before leaving the party in 1977 [[wikipedia]].

chapters.title: Socialist mayor and House independent
chapters.dek: A 10-vote win in Burlington and 16 years in the House.
chapters.body: In 1981 Sanders was elected mayor of Burlington by 22 votes, cut to 10 on a recount, and was reelected three times before leaving in 1989 [[wikipedia, sanders-senate-bio]]. Elected Vermont's at-large representative in 1990, he co-founded the Congressional Progressive Caucus in 1991 and served 16 years in the House as an independent [[wikipedia, sanders-senate-bio]].

chapters.title: The Senate
chapters.dek: Committee gavels on veterans, the budget and health.
chapters.body: Sanders entered the Senate in January 2007 and is now in his fourth term, the longest-serving independent in congressional history by his office's count [[wikipedia, sanders-senate-bio]]. As chairman of the Veterans' Affairs Committee he passed a 2014 overhaul of VA health care; he later chaired the Budget Committee (2021–2023) and the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee (2023–2025), where he is now ranking member [[sanders-senate-bio, wikipedia]].

chapters.title: Two presidential campaigns
chapters.dek: Runner-up twice, and leader of the party's left.
chapters.body: In 2016 Sanders challenged Hillary Clinton for the Democratic nomination and finished second, winning 23 primaries and caucuses [[wikipedia]]. At a March 2016 debate in Flint, asked whether he kept his Jewish identity in the background, he said, "I am very proud of being Jewish and that is an essential part of who I am as a human being" [[toi-jewish-2016]]. He ran again in 2020, finished second to Joe Biden, and became a close Biden ally [[wikipedia]].

chapters.title: Fighting Oligarchy
chapters.dek: Rally tours and kingmaking in the second Trump term.
chapters.body:
In February 2025 Sanders began the Fighting Oligarchy tour against the second Trump administration, later co-headlined by Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. It drew 34,000 people in Denver and 36,000 in Los Angeles that spring and about 261,000 in all by November 2025, and continued through the 2026 midterms [[wikipedia-tour]].

He used his standing to shape primaries. In June 2025 he endorsed Zohran Mamdani for mayor of New York, saying, "We need a new politics and new leadership" [[cbs-mamdani-2025]]. He backed Graham Platner in Maine's Senate race from its launch, then on July 7, 2026, after a sexual-assault allegation, said, "I have recommended that he step aside" [[wcax-platner-2026]]. In late October 2026 he was rallying for Democratic candidates in Minnesota, arguing that Trump's policies were "designed to make the richest people in America richer" [[nnn-duluth-2026]].

chapters.title: Blocking arms for Israel
chapters.dek: From a handful of votes to most of the Democratic caucus.
chapters.body: Since the Gaza war Sanders has repeatedly forced Senate votes on resolutions to block U.S. arms sales to Israel. They have all failed, but Democratic support has grown: 18 Democrats in November 2024, 27 in July 2025 on a resolution covering rifles, and in April 2026 40 members of the Democratic caucus on a resolution to block sales of bulldozers, with a companion resolution on 1,000-pound bombs failing 36–63 [[ap-arms-2025, intercept-arms-2026]]. "This is where the American people are," he said; "I think the Democrats have caught on to that" [[intercept-arms-2026]].
